title: What is gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protocol Buffers RPC), its advantages/disadvantages, use cases, and comparison with REST?
shortTitle: What is gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protocol Buffers RPC), its advantages/disadvantages, use cases, and comparison with REST?

s1_definition.profdef: gRPC is a high-performance, contract-first Remote Procedure Call framework that runs over HTTP/2 and serializes messages with Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format. You define services and messages in a `.proto` file, and a code generator produces strongly typed client stubs and server skeletons in many languages. gRPC supports four call types — unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming — and leverages HTTP/2 features like multiplexing, header compression, and full-duplex streaming for efficiency. It is widely used for internal microservice-to-microservice communication where performance, strong typing, and a shared contract matter.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's departments agreeing on a single official form template (the `.proto` contract) that every department must use, written once and automatically printed in every language the departments speak. When the transfers department wants the accounts department to do something, it fills the exact agreed form and calls a specific function by name, like "debitAccount," as if calling a local method. The forms are tiny, pre-compressed shorthand (Protocol Buffers) instead of bulky paragraphs (JSON), and the phone line between departments can carry many calls at once on one wire (HTTP/2 multiplexing). Everyone shares one contract, so misunderstandings are caught before the call even happens.
s1_definition.oneliner: gRPC is contract-first binary RPC over HTTP/2 using Protocol Buffers, giving fast, strongly typed, streaming-capable service-to-service calls.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** gRPC is a high-performance, contract-first Remote Procedure Call framework that runs over HTTP/2 and serializes messages with Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format. You define services and messages in a `.proto` file, and a code generator produces strongly typed client stubs and server skeletons in many languages. gRPC supports four call types — unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming — and leverages HTTP/2 features like multiplexing, header compression, and full-duplex streaming for efficiency. It is widely used for internal microservice-to-microservice communication where performance, strong typing, and a shared contract matter.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's departments agreeing on a single official form template (the `.proto` contract) that every department must use, written once and automatically printed in every language the departments speak. When the transfers department wants the accounts department to do something, it fills the exact agreed form and calls a specific function by name, like "debitAccount," as if calling a local method. The forms are tiny, pre-compressed shorthand (Protocol Buffers) instead of bulky paragraphs (JSON), and the phone line between departments can carry many calls at once on one wire (HTTP/2 multiplexing). Everyone shares one contract, so misunderstandings are caught before the call even happens.

**One line to remember:** gRPC is contract-first binary RPC over HTTP/2 using Protocol Buffers, giving fast, strongly typed, streaming-capable service-to-service calls.

sections.s2_technical:
You start with a `.proto` file that declares messages and a service with RPC methods. For example a service `AccountService` with `rpc Transfer(TransferRequest) returns (TransferResponse)`, where the messages list typed fields with numbered tags. The Protocol Buffers compiler generates client stubs and server base classes, so calling a remote method feels like calling a local one: `blockingStub.transfer(request)` returns a typed response. Protocol Buffers serialize to a compact binary form using the field numbers, which is far smaller and faster to parse than JSON, and the numbered fields are what enable safe schema evolution.

gRPC defines four method kinds. Unary is one request and one response, like a classic call. Server streaming sends one request and receives a stream of responses, good for a feed. Client streaming sends a stream of requests and gets one response, good for uploads or aggregation. Bidirectional streaming streams both ways at once over one call. These all ride on HTTP/2, which multiplexes many concurrent streams over a single connection, compresses headers with HPACK, and supports full-duplex streaming, so gRPC avoids the head-of-line and per-request overhead that plague HTTP/1.1.

Advantages: high performance and low bandwidth from binary Protocol Buffers; strong typing and a single source-of-truth contract that generates clients in many languages; built-in streaming; first-class deadlines, cancellation, and metadata; and excellent fit for polyglot microservices. Disadvantages: it is not human-readable like JSON, so debugging needs tooling (grpcurl, reflection); limited native browser support, requiring gRPC-Web and a proxy; it requires HTTP/2 end to end, which some older proxies and load balancers handle poorly; and it has a steeper learning curve and build-time code generation. Use cases: internal east-west microservice communication, low-latency high-throughput APIs, streaming telemetry or market data, and polyglot systems needing one contract. Comparison with REST: REST over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 typically uses JSON, is resource-oriented and human-readable, is trivially consumable from browsers and curl, and has enormous ecosystem support, but it is more verbose, has no enforced schema by default, and lacks native bidirectional streaming. gRPC is action/method-oriented RPC, binary and compact, strongly typed by contract, and streaming-capable, but less browser-friendly and less human-readable. A senior nuance: I use gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where performance and a shared contract matter, and REST for public, browser-facing, or partner APIs where ubiquity and readability win, and I often expose a REST or gRPC-Web gateway in front of internal gRPC services.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service must call the account service millions of times a day with minimal latency and a guaranteed shared contract. JSON over HTTP/1.1 is too verbose and has no enforced schema. This is exactly what gRPC solves — a compact binary contract-first call that feels like a local method.

Problem 2 — The services are written in different languages across teams, and the contract must stay consistent everywhere. This is exactly what a `.proto` contract plus code generation provides — one contract, generated stubs in every language.

The demo defines an `AccountService` proto with a unary `Transfer` RPC, implements the server, and calls it from a client stub to move money from Rajesh to Priya. Classes and steps: `account.proto` (contract), `AccountServiceImpl` (server), `GrpcServer` (bootstraps), and `TransferClient` (calls the stub).
sections.s4a_structure:
```
grpc-account-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── proto/
│   │   │   └── account.proto               (the contract)
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/grpc/
│   │   │   ├── GrpcServer.java             (starts the server)
│   │   │   ├── AccountServiceImpl.java     (server implementation)
│   │   │   └── TransferClient.java         (client stub call)
│   │   └── resources/

│   └── test/

```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (protobuf-maven-plugin generates stubs from account.proto)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run server
java -cp target/classes com.bank.grpc.GrpcServer

# Run client (separate terminal)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.grpc.TransferClient

# Inspect with grpcurl (binary protocol needs tooling)
grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"from_account":"SAV2001","to_account":"CUR3001","amount":"50000","idempotency_key":"k1"}' \
  localhost:9090 bank.AccountService/Transfer
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1 — The client builds a `TransferRequest` using the generated builder. The fields are serialized to compact Protocol Buffers binary using their field numbers, not field names, so the payload is tiny.

Step 2 — The call travels over HTTP/2 as a single multiplexed stream to the server. The blocking stub makes it feel like a local method call despite being a network RPC.

Step 3 — `AccountServiceImpl.transfer` parses the amount into BigDecimal, checks Rajesh has enough, debits SAV2001 to Rs.950,000 and credits CUR3001 to Rs.300,000, then sends one response and completes the call.

Step 4 — The binary response is deserialized by the generated client code into a typed `TransferResponse`, and the client logs the completed status and both balances. The whole round trip used a compact binary contract both sides agreed on at build time.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] gRPC AccountService on 9090
2026-10-26 14:55:12 [INFO] gRPC Transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 14:55:12 [INFO] Status=COMPLETED Rajesh=Rs.950000 Priya=Rs.300000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  TransferClient (generated blocking stub)
    │ build TransferRequest → Protobuf binary (field numbers, compact)
    ▼ HTTP/2 stream (multiplexed, HPACK headers)
  AccountServiceImpl.transfer(req, StreamObserver)
    │ amount = BigDecimal("50000")
    │ SAV2001: 1,000,000 → 950,000   (debit)
    │ CUR3001:   250,000 → 300,000   (credit)
    │ obs.onNext(TransferResponse) ; obs.onCompleted()
    ▼ HTTP/2 response stream → Protobuf decode
  Client logs: COMPLETED, Rajesh Rs.950,000, Priya Rs.300,000

  Contract (account.proto) → protoc → stubs in Java/Go/Python (one source of truth)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — gRPC Microservice Mesh ═══

  ┌──────────┐ REST/gRPC-Web ┌──────────────┐ gRPC ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Browser  │──────────────→│ API Gateway  │─────→│ Transfer Svc (×N) │
  │ / Mobile │               │ (Envoy)      │ HTTP/2│                  │
  └──────────┘               └──────────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘
                                                            │ gRPC unary
                                                            ▼
                                                  ┌──────────────────┐ JDBC ┌────────────┐
                                                  │ Account Svc (×N)  │─────→│ PostgreSQL │
                                                  └──────────────────┘      └────────────┘
  Internal east-west = gRPC (binary, contract). Public edge = REST/gRPC-Web.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — gRPC Contract-First Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Contract-First (IDL): .proto is the single source of truth     │
  │    WHY: generated stubs keep all languages in sync             │
  │ Stub/Proxy: client stub hides the network call                 │
  │    WHY: remote call feels like a local method                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: AccountServiceImpl only does account operations             │
  │ O: add rpc method = extend proto, regenerate, no edits to old  │
  │ L: generated stub honors the service contract                  │
  │ D: client depends on generated interface, not transport        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Method Kinds (as prose) ───────────────────────────────────
  unary          : 1 req → 1 resp   (Transfer)
  server-stream  : 1 req → N resp   (statement feed)
  client-stream  : N req → 1 resp   (bulk upload)
  bidi-stream    : N req ↔ N resp   (live reconciliation)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. stub.transfer(TransferRequest)  → Protobuf encode → HTTP/2
  2.   → AccountServiceImpl.transfer(req, obs)
  3.   → debit/credit → obs.onNext(resp) → obs.onCompleted()
  4.   → client decodes TransferResponse
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
gRPC is a high-performance, contract-first remote procedure call framework that runs over HTTP/2 and serializes messages with Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format. I define my services and messages once in a proto file, and a code generator produces strongly typed client stubs and server skeletons in many languages, so calling a remote service feels like calling a local method. It supports four call types, unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming, and it rides on HTTP/2 features like multiplexing many concurrent streams over one connection, header compression, and full-duplex streaming.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I used gRPC for the high-volume internal call from the transfer service to the account service. The proto file is the single shared contract, money is carried as a string and parsed into BigDecimal so we never use floating point, and each field has a stable number that gives us compact wire encoding and safe schema evolution. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya is a unary call that debits and credits the accounts and returns the new balances, and because the stub is generated, the transfer team and the account team, even in different languages, always agree on the contract.

The advantages I emphasize are high performance and low bandwidth from binary Protocol Buffers, strong typing with a single source of truth, built-in streaming, and first-class deadlines and cancellation, which makes it ideal for internal microservice communication and polyglot systems. The disadvantages are that it is not human-readable so debugging needs tooling like grpcurl, browsers need gRPC-Web and a proxy, it requires HTTP/2 end to end which some older infrastructure handles poorly, and it has build-time code generation and a steeper learning curve.

Comparing it with REST, REST is resource-oriented, usually JSON, human-readable, trivially consumable from browsers and curl, and has a huge ecosystem, but it is verbose, has no enforced schema by default, and lacks native bidirectional streaming. gRPC is method-oriented, binary, strongly typed by contract, and streaming-capable, but less browser-friendly. So my rule, which I state in interviews, is: use gRPC for internal east-west service calls where performance and a shared contract matter, use REST for public, browser-facing, or partner APIs where ubiquity and readability win, and put a REST or gRPC-Web gateway in front of internal gRPC services when the edge needs it.
